strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation issue for brain-to-text generation: repeated stimuli and overlapping signal windows can make benchmark scores misleading about generalization to new subjects and content.

The subject–task–text–signal representation and visual comparison of splitting strategies help explain these dependencies. Jointly withholding subjects and stimuli is a sensible evaluation target, and grouping fMRI samples by story addresses overlapping text windows.

Experiments cover Narratives and ZuCo using established decoding models. Four seeds for overlap measurements and the training details in Appendix A provide useful foundations for a reproducible evaluation study.
weaknesses: The supplied algorithms do not enforce the central separation guarantee as written. Algorithm 1, line 15, restores edges after checking the subject endpoint but never excludes text assigned to validation or test. Thus, an edge connecting a training subject to held-out text can reintroduce stimulus overlap. Algorithm 2, line 33, has the symmetric omission for subjects. The sampling direction in Algorithm 1 also conflicts with Section 3.3. These inconsistencies must be reconciled with the reported zero-leakage results.

Reported metrics contain substantive inconsistencies. Table 4 gives EEG2Text ROUGE-1 recall 23.98, precision 23.95, and F1 25.74; standard F1 cannot exceed both precision and recall under consistent aggregation. Table 3 contains similar cases. Additionally, Equation 8 measures overlap of identical signal elements, whereas the stated subject-separation criterion excludes any recording from the same subject. The metric definitions, implementation, and tables need verification.

The experiments do not establish the claimed mechanisms of overfitting and memorization. Section 5.2 treats improving test scores or decreasing reconstruction validation loss as evidence of leakage, although neither trend is diagnostic. The UniCoRN/UniCoRN* comparison simultaneously changes initialization, learning rate, and training duration. A randomly initialized but trainable encoder is also not a control for whether brain information matters. Matched comparisons and text-only or shuffled-signal controls are needed to support the strong claims about decoder memorization and limited encoder usefulness.

The manuscript conflates different generalization targets with data leakage. Evaluating new text from previously observed subjects can be legitimate for personalized decoding; evaluating new subjects on familiar stimuli addresses another legitimate target. The proposed joint holdout is appropriate for its stated goal, but this does not establish that all alternative protocols are inherently invalid. Claims about prior work should be qualified by the evaluation target and demonstrated overlap.

The claimed improvement in dataset utilization is unsupported. The paper acknowledges discarding data but does not report retained and discarded sample counts, achieved partition sizes, or comparisons with simpler joint holdout procedures. Restoring allowable edges under one chosen assignment does not establish maximum utilization. Splitting subjects or tasks in an 8:1:1 ratio also does not necessarily produce that ratio in samples.

Reproducibility remains insufficient for the claimed benchmark release. The manuscript provides no code or split-download link, exact subject/task assignments, or partition counts after filtering and discarding data. Test-time decoding and checkpoint selection need clearer specification, and decoding results lack variability across splits or training runs—particularly consequential with only 12 ZuCo participants. These gaps, together with the algorithm and metric inconsistencies, prevent a sound Findings recommendation and motivate resubmission after correction and validation.
